title: Hepatitis B reactivation after switch to injectable treatment: rare, but proceed with caution - Aidsmap

analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-11-19. Event date: Not reported in the supplied evidence. Time range: Follow-up periods of 25 months in Spain and 2.7 years in Italy.
analysis.location_and_population: Affected population: People living with HIV, particularly those with past exposure to hepatitis B or potential hidden, low-level infection.
analysis.event: Hepatitis B reactivation was observed in some individuals after switching to injectable treatment regimens containing cabotegravir / rilpivirine. This was reported by studies presented at the International Congress on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection (HIV Glasgow 2026).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In Spain, 115 people had isolated anti-HBc detected during follow-up, but no clinically suspected reactivation with liver enzyme elevations was observed. analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Studies suggest that reactivation is rare, but regular monitoring is recommended. analysis.brief_en: This news report highlights the risk of hepatitis B reactivation in people living with HIV after switching to injectable treatment regimens containing cabotegravir / rilpivirine. Studies presented at the International Congress on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection (HIV Glasgow 2026) found that reactivation rates were low or non-existent in cohort studies conducted in Spain and Italy. In Spain, the RELATIVITY cohort followed 3349 individuals who switched to injectable treatment before the end of 2024, with a median follow-up of 25 months. No clinically suspected reactivation with liver enzyme elevations was observed, but 115 participants had isolated anti-HBc detected. In Italy, the SCohoLART study followed 627 individuals, with 30% having previous HBV exposure. Four HBV-related events were reported, including one case of symptomatic reactivation requiring hospitalisation. The report notes that the risk of reactivation appears low with dolutegravir / lamivudine, but the evidence is not sufficient to confirm protection. Regular monitoring is recommended due to the unpredictability of reactivation. HBV DNA testing was not routinely performed, which may have underestimated reactivation cases.

It was tested on 23,098 participants across three cohorts: modeling (1,533), internal validation (657), and external validation (20,908). The GADA model showed strong performance, with AUCs ranging from 0.858 to 0.977 and sensitivity of 86.00% and specificity of 81.88% in the external validation. The model is designed to distinguish HBV-related HCC from chronic hepatitis B and HBV-related cirrhosis, reducing testing complexity and improving accessibility in resource-limited settings.
